notes:
THE ETHICAL VISION OF JESUS (Section D: Moral Decision-making, Chapter 4)

OPENING QUOTE
- "The love of our neighbour is the only door out of the dungeon of self." (George MacDonald)

HOW VALUES ARE PASSED ON
- Reflective exercise: draw the people who influenced you, with the most important nearest, and note the values you admire in them (e.g. a grandparent who kept the family close; an aunt who worked for Trócaire in Africa with a great sense of justice).
- People communicate values mostly by THE WAY THEY ARE and THE WAY THEY LIVE - how they react to adversity and joy - as much as by what they say. You may forget what a teacher said but remember their qualities.
- In the same way, JESUS TEACHES BY HIS LIFE; HIS LIFE IS THE MESSAGE. His ethical vision flows from his PERSON, his LIFE and his TEACHING.
- His ethical teaching is found in laws and rules, stories and parables, but MOST IMPORTANTLY IN THE PERSON OF JESUS.

READING THE TEXTS WITH CARE
- When we read the gospels or Paul's letters we are reading an INTERPRETATION of Jesus' teaching, written for a particular community and shaped by the writer.
- It is very challenging to give an accurate account of Jesus' ethics; we can draw a picture of the main thrusts.
- There is HARDLY ANY ETHICAL MATERIAL IN MARK, whereas MATTHEW and LUKE have included moral teaching in their gospels.

METANOIA: REPENT AND BELIEVE
- Jesus began his preaching: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news." (Mark 1:15)
- It is a CALL TO CONVERSION and a DEMAND TO BELIEVE. God has issued an invitation; our response must be: repent and believe - we must do BOTH. Then the kingdom can grow in our lives.
- METANOIA (Greek): a CHANGE OF MIND - what happens when a person repents and believes. Jesus calls for a FUNDAMENTAL REORIENTATION of one's life.
- When people respond with repentance and faith, God's healing flows.
- (Catholics hear "Turn away from sin, and believe in the gospel!" spoken to them individually - a question in the chapter asks on which day; an assignment suggests researching rugby player Jason Robinson.)

REPENTANCE
- The parables of LUKE 15, especially the PRODIGAL SON, show God's JOY at the repentance of sinners.
- Jesus has not come to call the righteous, but SINNERS.
- The OPPOSITE of repentance is PRIDE and ARROGANCE. God will exalt the humble and bring down the proud (Luke 14:11). The arrogant "will not have ears to hear" (Matthew 11). Even God cannot work with those unwilling to hear.

FAITH
- "Your faith has made you well." (Mark 5:34)
- The miracles, SIGNS OF THE KINGDOM, only happen when there is faith. With faith in God anything can happen (Mark 5:34, 9:14-29; Luke 7:9). Without faith, Christ's grace cannot act (Mark 6:5).
- REPENTANCE AND FAITH are the CORNERSTONES of Christian life, the key dynamic.

THE KINGDOM OF GOD
- The CENTRAL THEME in Jesus' teaching. All else flows from it.
- The kingdom is the RULE OF GOD, present now and which will prevail when God's kingdom is fully established. Also called the REIGN OF GOD.
- Best described by Jesus in his PARABLES, which take the form of a question and an image: "What shall the Kingdom of God be like? It is like..." (see Mark 4:26-32). They show the radical nature of following the kingdom.

GRACE
- Christians meet Jesus through his words in scripture, and believe the RISEN CHRIST is with them and active in their lives, especially through the SACRAMENTS.
- This action of God is called GRACE. Living in grace enables people to live out the demands of the gospel; God's grace can guide them if they are open to it.

LAW
- The LAW OF MOSES was very important to the Jews, but often stressed the LETTER of the law over HUMAN NEED.
- Luke 6:1-11: keeping the Sabbath had become more important than healing people.
- Jesus did NOT abandon the Old Law, but he rejected the LEGALISM of the PHARISEES.
- Jesus FULFILLED the law by being faithful to its ROOTS, not its strict interpretation.

SO WHAT'S NEW WITH JESUS?
- The command to love is at the heart of Jesus' teaching, but it is NOT ENTIRELY NEW: it is in the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 6:4-5). The Jews had this text on their foreheads and doorposts.
- "I give you a new commandment, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also should love one another." (John 13:34)
- "For you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another." (1 Thessalonians 4:9)
- WHAT IS NEW IS CHRIST HIMSELF: his person, life, death and resurrection, sayings, miracles and relationship with us are all central to Christian morality.
- We cannot talk about Jesus' ethics without talking about who he is, what he did and what he said. The Christian's moral life is bound up in their RELATIONSHIP WITH CHRIST - a living response to God's love shown in Christ.
- What is new: THE KINGDOM HAS COME and God is truly here; the revelation of God's love is before us in Christ.

THE COMMANDMENT OF LOVE
- All of Jesus' moral teaching is concentrated in one command: LOVE - of GOD and of NEIGHBOUR.
- The authorities tried to catch him out: "Which commandment is the first of all?" Jesus answered: the first is "Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one; you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength." The second: "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." "There is no other commandment greater than these." (Mark 12:28-34)
- Compare: Luke 10:25-28; Matthew 22:34-40; Deuteronomy 6:4-5; Leviticus 19:18.
- It is a SUCCINCT SUMMARY OF THE DECALOGUE: the FIRST THREE commands express LOVE OF GOD; the FINAL SEVEN express LOVE OF NEIGHBOUR.
- St Augustine: "Love and do what you will."
- JOHN'S GOSPEL uses symbolism and images. At the LAST SUPPER Jesus WASHES HIS DISCIPLES' FEET, giving himself as an example of UNCONDITIONAL LOVE, then gives the new commandment (John 13:34-35).

AGAPE - TYPES OF LOVE IN GREEK
- In English "love" has lost power because it is used for everything (mushrooms, TV, my father, my wife).
- Greek, the language of the New Testament, has different words:
- EROS: sexual attraction and love.
- PHILIA: the love of friendship.
- STORGE: the love of affection.
- AGAPE: UNSELFISH love, seeking only the good of the other; often translated "CHARITY".
- Self-giving, selfless agape is CENTRAL to Jesus' moral law.

THE SERMON ON THE MOUNT (Matthew 5-7)
Context
- Put together by MATTHEW, who wrote a very structured gospel for a JEWISH COMMUNITY, based on MARK's gospel.
- Matthew balances the Old Law, still present, with a NEW STRINGENCY brought by Jesus.
- In LUKE it appears as the SERMON ON THE PLAIN.
- It was one of MAHATMA GANDHI's favourite texts; he admonished Christians for neglecting it.
Teaching
- The MOST CONCISE moral teaching of Jesus and the clearest, most RADICAL expression of what it means to live as a Christian.
- Begins with the BEATITUDES: blessed are the poor, the meek, the merciful, those who mourn. The POWERLESS in this world are blessed in the kingdom.
- "Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you... If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also."
- Shocking imagery: "If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away."
- There is URGENCY in its language and tone, and a choice: to be great or least in the kingdom.
- Everything in the worldly order is TURNED ON ITS HEAD.
- Key theme: Jesus looks at what is WITHIN. MORALITY IS INTERNAL. Your motives are how you will be judged.
- The Old Law laid down a rule; the sermon DEEPENS it and makes it INTERNAL. Jesus is not abolishing the Old Law but deepening it.
- CCC 1968: the Sermon on the Mount, "far from abolishing or devaluing the moral prescriptions of the Old Law, releases their hidden potential and shows how new demands arise from them."
- Matthew 5:21-48 has six statements in the form "You have heard that it was said... But I say to you..."

IMPOSSIBLE DEMANDS?
- Joke: many a sermon goes over people's heads and hits someone else!
- How can one avoid anger? Should you cut off a hand? Is the sermon useless because it asks the impossible? Some interpretations:
- A PRAYER RATHER THAN AN ETHIC: counsels/advice, not commands - spirituality, so not everyone must follow it; "we follow the Ten Commandments, and pray the sermon."
- AN IDEAL: to aim at, seeking higher values, but impossible to live in the real world.
- But the Fathers of the Church said the sermon was FOR EVERYONE:
- AUGUSTINE called it the PERFECT PATTERN for Christian life.
- THOMAS AQUINAS said it contains ALL THE INFORMATION NEEDED for the Christian life.
- POPE JOHN PAUL II, in VERITATIS SPLENDOR, called it the MAGNA CHARTA OF CHRISTIAN MORALITY.
- If morality is a PATH TO HAPPINESS, not just a list of commands, the sermon makes sense: it points to true, fulfilling happiness. It is a prayer AND an ideal AND a way to fulfilment.

KEY PRINCIPLES IN JESUS' ETHICAL VISION (DONAL HARRINGTON'S SIX THEMES)
1. THE MINIMUM AND THE MORE: a morality of the MORE - going far beyond what the law requires; think of what I MIGHT do, not what I HAVE to do (Matthew 5:21-48). Key point: give the maximum, give everything.
2. THE EXTERNAL AND THE INTERNAL: do good - prayer, almsgiving, fasting - IN PRIVATE, not just to be seen. Moral judgement takes place in the HEART, a private meeting place with God. T.S. Eliot (Murder in the Cathedral): "The Last Temptation is the Greatest Treason: to do the right deed for the wrong reason." Key point: what is inside is important.
3. PRINCIPLES AND PEOPLE: Jesus is ON THE SIDE OF PEOPLE. "The Sabbath was made for humankind, not humankind for the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27). The moral law exists to promote people's wellbeing. Key point: people are first.
4. THE LETTER AND THE SPIRIT: the SPIRIT of the moral law is LOVE. "If you do not have love, you have nothing at all." "What I want is mercy, not sacrifice." Key point: love is primary.
5. SELF-RIGHTEOUSNESS AND HUMILITY: only the HUMBLE, who know where they stand with God, see God's grace at work (Luke 18:9-14). Self-righteousness blocks the moral life. Key point: humility opens the person to God.
6. ATTACHMENT AND DETACHMENT: morality is SINGLE-MINDEDNESS. "Where our heart lies, there will our treasure be also." Choose God or the world, wealth or the kingdom (Matthew 6:24; 12:25; Luke 9:62; Luke 19:1-10). Preoccupation with worldly concerns makes us lose sight of God and fills life with anxiety. Key point: we must be free from the world to follow God.

ST PAUL AND ETHICS
- PAUL's writings were the FIRST BOOKS of the New Testament to be written; the gospels came a little later. So they give the VERY FIRST teaching of the Church on moral life.
- Paul's ethics is rooted in FAITH IN CHRIST - a CHRISTOCENTRIC view: Christ is at the centre.
- "Let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus." (Philippians 2:5)
- The Jews speak of JUSTICE, the Greeks of WISDOM; for Christians all truth comes from a CRUCIFIED AND RISEN CHRIST in the Spirit.
- The Christian is GUIDED BY THE SPIRIT (Galatians 5) toward goodness and away from self-indulgence.
- First command is love: "there are three things that last: faith, hope and love. And the greatest of these is love." (1 Corinthians 13; also Galatians 5:6, 1 John 4:20)

THE RICH YOUNG MAN (Mark 10:17-31; Matthew 19:16-30; Luke 18:18-30)
- He asks: "Teacher, what good must I do to have eternal life?" Jesus: "There is only one who is good. If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments."
- Jesus lists: do not murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness; honour father and mother; love your neighbour as yourself.
- The young man: "I have kept all these; what do I still lack?" Jesus: "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me." (Matthew 19:16-21)
- Matthew does not name the young man.
- VERITATIS SPLENDOR: in the young man we recognise EVERY PERSON who questions Christ about morality. His question is not so much about rules but about THE FULL MEANING OF LIFE - an appeal to the ABSOLUTE GOOD, "the echo of a call from God, who is the origin and goal of our life."
- What held him back from loving fully was his RICHES. You can know all the commandments but still need to LET GO radically to follow Christ. It is deeper than knowing the truth - you must DO THE TRUTH.

SUMMARY
- Christ preaches the Kingdom of God. God's grace helps people live Christian lives.
- Metanoia means change of mind; Christ's first call is to repent and believe. Those without repentance or faith will not enter the kingdom.
- The central Christian ethic is the command of love: love God and love neighbour.
- The model is the Sermon on the Mount: a challenging but inspiring Magna Charta for moral life.
- Key elements: doing the maximum, pure reasons for actions, respecting people's dignity, keeping love central, humility, and detachment.
- Richard Nixon quote for discussion: "People react to fear, not love - they don't teach that in Sunday school, but it's true."

KEY TERMS
- Metanoia: Greek for change of mind; the fundamental reorientation of life when a person repents and believes.
- Repentance: turning away from sin; its opposite is pride and arrogance.
- The Kingdom of God: the rule or reign of God, present now and to be fully established; the central theme of Jesus' teaching.
- Grace: the action of God, especially through the sacraments, enabling people to live the gospel.
- Agape: unselfish love seeking only the good of the other ("charity").

rows.prompt: What is metanoia? Explain why both repentance and faith are needed.
rows.model_answer: Metanoia is Greek for a change of mind - the fundamental reorientation of life when a person repents and believes. Jesus said 'repent, and believe in the good news' (Mark 1:15). Both are needed: the proud cannot hear God, and without faith Christ's grace cannot act; together they are the cornerstones of Christian life.

rows.prompt: Explain Jesus' attitude to the Law of Moses.
rows.model_answer: Jesus did not abandon the Old Law, but he rejected the legalism of the Pharisees, which put the letter of the law above human need - as when keeping the Sabbath mattered more than healing (Luke 6:1-11). He fulfilled the law by being faithful to its roots rather than its strict interpretation.

rows.prompt: What is the law of love, according to Jesus?
rows.model_answer: The first commandment is to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength. The second is to love your neighbour as yourself. There is no greater commandment (Mark 12:28-34).

rows.prompt: Name the four Greek words for love and explain agape.
rows.model_answer: Eros is sexual attraction, philia is friendship, storge is affection and agape is unselfish love. Agape seeks only the good of the other and is often translated 'charity'. This self-giving love is central to Jesus' moral law.

rows.prompt: List three sayings from the Sermon on the Mount.
rows.model_answer: 'Blessed are the poor, the meek, the merciful, those who mourn.' 'Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you.' 'If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also.'

rows.prompt: Describe two ways people have interpreted the 'impossible demands' of the Sermon on the Mount, and the Church Fathers' view.
rows.model_answer: Some see it as a prayer rather than an ethic - advice, not commands, so we follow the Ten Commandments and pray the sermon. Others see it as an ideal that cannot be lived in the real world. But Augustine called it the perfect pattern for Christian life and said it was for everyone.

rows.prompt: Name Donal Harrington's six key themes in Jesus' ethical teaching.
rows.model_answer: The Minimum and the More; the External and the Internal; Principles and People; the Letter and the Spirit; Self-righteousness and Humility; and Attachment and Detachment.

rows.topic_label: St Paul and the rich young man
rows.prompt: What is the rich young man's question really about, according to Veritatis splendor?
rows.model_answer: It is not so much about rules to follow but about the full meaning of life. It is an appeal to the absolute Good, 'the echo of a call from God, who is the origin and goal of our life'. In him we recognise every person who questions Christ about morality.

rows.prompt: 'The Sermon on the Mount is the Magna Charta of Christian morality.' Discuss this statement. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Pope John Paul II called the sermon the Magna Charta of Christian morality in Veritatis splendor. Matthew put it together for a Jewish community, balancing the Old Law with a new stringency brought by Jesus; Luke has it as the Sermon on the Plain. It is Jesus' most concise and radical moral teaching. It begins with the Beatitudes: blessed are the poor, the meek, the merciful and those who mourn, so the powerless are blessed in the kingdom. It asks us to love our enemies and turn the other cheek, and uses shocking images: 'If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out.' There is urgency, and everything worldly is turned on its head. Above all, morality becomes internal: Jesus looks at what is within, at our motives. He does not abolish the Old Law but deepens it; the CCC (1968) says it 'releases their hidden potential'. Some call its demands impossible, seeing it as a prayer rather than an ethic or an unreachable ideal. But Augustine called it the perfect pattern for Christian life, Aquinas said it contains all that is needed, and Gandhi admonished Christians for neglecting it. If morality is a path to true happiness, the sermon makes sense: it is a prayer, an ideal and a way to fulfilment.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: Veritatis splendor; Matthew/Jewish community/Sermon on the Plain; Beatitudes; love enemies, turn cheek; shocking imagery and urgency; internal morality; deepening not abolishing Old Law, CCC 1968; prayer/ideal interpretations; Augustine, Aquinas, Gandhi; path to happiness.

rows.prompt: Outline the key principles in Jesus' ethical vision as identified by Donal Harrington. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Donal Harrington identified six key themes. First, the Minimum and the More: Jesus asks for a morality of the more, going far beyond what the law requires - thinking of what I might do, not what I have to do (Matthew 5:21-48). Give everything. Second, the External and the Internal: prayer, almsgiving and fasting should be done in private, not to be seen. Moral judgement takes place in the heart, a meeting place with God. T.S. Eliot warns against doing 'the right deed for the wrong reason'. Third, Principles and People: Jesus is on the side of people. 'The Sabbath was made for humankind, not humankind for the Sabbath' (Mark 2:27); the law exists for people's wellbeing. Fourth, the Letter and the Spirit: the spirit of the law is love. 'What I want is mercy, not sacrifice.' Fifth, Self-righteousness and Humility: only the humble, who know where they stand with God, see God's grace at work (Luke 18:9-14); self-righteousness blocks moral life. Sixth, Attachment and Detachment: morality is single-mindedness. We must choose God or the world, wealth or the kingdom; worldly preoccupation fills life with anxiety. In short: give the maximum, what is inside matters, people come first, love is primary, humility opens us to God, and we must be free from the world to follow God.
rows.marking_scheme: Six principles x (name 1 mark + explanation/example 2 marks) = 18; summary or overall linking 2 marks.

rows.prompt: 'What is new in the new commandment is Christ himself.' Explain this statement. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: The command to love is at the heart of Jesus' teaching, but it is not entirely new. Deuteronomy 6:4-5 already commanded love of God, and the Jews wore this text on their foreheads and doorposts; Leviticus 19:18 commands love of neighbour. In John 13:34 Jesus says, 'I give you a new commandment, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also should love one another.' What is new is Christ himself: his person, life, death and resurrection, sayings, miracles and relationship with us. At the Last Supper he washed his disciples' feet as an example of unconditional love. The Christian's moral life is bound up in their relationship with Christ, a living response to God's love shown in him. In Christ the kingdom has come and God is truly here.
rows.marking_scheme: Love command found in Old Testament 3 marks; John 13:34 quoted/explained 2 marks; Christ's person, life, death and resurrection as the new element 3 marks; relationship with Christ/kingdom has come 2 marks.

rows.topic_label: St Paul and the rich young man
rows.prompt: What does the story of the rich young man teach about Christian morality? (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The story is in Mark 10, Matthew 19 and Luke 18. A young man asks Jesus, 'Teacher, what good must I do to have eternal life?' Jesus tells him to keep the commandments: not to murder, commit adultery, steal or bear false witness, to honour his father and mother, and to love his neighbour as himself. The young man says he has kept all these and asks, 'What do I still lack?' Jesus answers, 'If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions, and give the money to the poor... then come, follow me.' Veritatis splendor says that in this unnamed man we recognise every person who questions Christ about morality. His question is not so much about rules as about the full meaning of life; it is an appeal to the absolute Good, the echo of God's call. The story teaches that keeping rules is the minimum; Jesus asks for the more. What held the young man back was his riches, which shows Harrington's principle of attachment and detachment: we must be free from the world to follow God. It is not enough to know the truth; we must do the truth by letting go radically to follow Christ.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: the story and dialogue; commandments listed; sell possessions and follow; Veritatis splendor - every person, meaning of life, absolute Good, call from God; riches held him back; minimum and the more; detachment; knowing vs doing the truth.

rows.prompt: Explain the place of repentance and faith in Jesus' preaching of the Kingdom of God. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: The central theme of Jesus' teaching is the Kingdom of God, the rule or reign of God, described in parables such as those in Mark 4:26-32. Jesus began his preaching: 'The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news' (Mark 1:15). This is a call to metanoia, a change of mind and a fundamental reorientation of life. Repentance means turning from sin; the Prodigal Son shows God's joy when sinners repent. Its opposite is pride: God exalts the humble and brings down the proud. Faith is also needed: 'Your faith has made you well' (Mark 5:34). Miracles, the signs of the kingdom, only happen where there is faith; without it Christ's grace cannot act. So repentance and faith are the cornerstones of Christian life, letting the kingdom grow in us.
rows.marking_scheme: Kingdom as central theme 2 marks; Mark 1:15 and metanoia 2 marks; repentance with example 2 marks; pride as opposite 1 mark; faith with example 2 marks; cornerstones 1 mark.
